analysis.one_liner: Restricts online payday-style lenders: state interest-rate caps apply, lenders must register, lead generators and hidden bank drafts are curbed, prepaid overdraft fees are banned.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tighten rules on small-dollar, high-cost loans — the kind marketed online as payday or installment loans. Lenders would have to register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and loans made over the internet or by national banks would have to follow the interest-rate and fee laws of the borrower's home state, closing a common workaround used to charge rates those state laws prohibit. It would also stop companies from pulling money out of a borrower's bank account without written permission, restrict the lead-generator websites that sell applicants' bank and Social Security information to lenders, ban overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, and order a study of small-dollar lending on tribal reservations [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who use small-dollar loans: they would keep the protections of their own state's lending laws no matter where the lender is located, could stop electronic withdrawals from their bank account, and would no longer face overdraft fees on prepaid accounts. Consumers would also gain a layer of privacy protection, since websites could no longer sell their bank account and Social Security information to lenders they do not actually lend through.

how_it_helps.text: Any small-dollar loan (roughly $5,000 or less, repaid in installments) made online, by phone, by mail, or by a national bank must comply with the annual percentage rate, interest, and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives [S3].

Small-dollar lenders must register with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau before issuing credit, and the definition covers not just lenders but anyone who brokers, arranges, or gathers applications for these loans [S2] [S3].

A borrower who agrees to repay a small-dollar loan by electronic fund transfer gets the same protections as any preauthorized transfer, including the right to stop payment, and remotely created checks can only be issued by a person the consumer designated in writing, with that designation given directly to the consumer's own bank [S2] [S3].
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts are prohibited, and transactions exceeding the account balance can be declined without a fee [S2] [S3].

Websites and brokers may not distribute sensitive personal financial information — Social Security numbers, bank account and routing numbers, access codes — in connection with a small-dollar loan unless they are directly making the loan, and they must disclose how they can be identified and served with legal process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online payday, installment, and tribal-entity lenders, lead-generation companies that sell loan applicants' financial data, prepaid card programs that charge overdraft fees, and the banks that process these loans would all lose revenue or face new compliance requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: High-cost online lenders and lead generators

drawbacks.text: Some borrowers use small-dollar loans when they cannot get credit elsewhere; if state rate caps make online lending unprofitable, fewer lenders may offer credit, and some borrowers could shift to less-regulated or black-market alternatives — the tradeoff every rate-cap proposal faces, even though the bill ordered a study of credit access rather than building in alternatives [S3].

The bill hands the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau broad rulemaking authority — to define which payment orders count as 'remotely created checks,' to define 'prepaid account,' to raise the $5,000 threshold, and to ban additional fees — which lenders and their allies argue gives one agency wide discretion over a large consumer credit market [S3].

A borrower could be held liable for any amount paid on a remotely created check despite the bank's refusal to pay, the same liability standard that already applies to unauthorized electronic fund transfers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are concrete and targeted at documented abuse patterns — unauthorized bank drafts, out-of-state rate evasion through internet loans or bank partnerships, and data-selling lead farms. The main cost is that tighter rules plus state rate caps could shrink the supply of legal small-dollar credit for people with no other options, a real risk the bill acknowledged only by ordering a study rather than a remedy. On balance the bill is a straightforward consumer-protection measure whose costs fall on lenders rather than borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, joined by Rep. Elijah Cummings as its only cosponsor [S1] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S5].
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; no markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-cost online lenders and lead-generation companies kept operating under the pre-existing rules, with no registration requirement, no state rate-cap application to internet loans, and no ban on prepaid overdraft fees.

for.name: Rep. Suzanne Bonamici
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole listed sponsor.

for.name: Rep. Elijah Cummings
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it attracted.

sides.party_line_note: No opposition is recorded and the bill died in committee without a vote, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested; its two supporters were both Democrats.

industries.industry: Online payday and small-dollar installment lenders
industries.note: The bill would require them to register with the CFPB and apply each borrower's home-state rate caps to internet and national-bank loans, eroding the fee and interest income that defines the business model. Borrowers would pay less for the same loans.

industries.industry: Lead generators and consumer-data brokers in lending
industries.note: The bill would bar anyone who is not the actual lender from handling loan applicants' Social Security and bank account information, cutting off a market in selling vulnerable borrowers' data. Consumers would get privacy protection instead.
Overdraft fees on prepaid accounts would be banned, removing a fee stream charged mainly to lower-income users of prepaid cards. The same users would save money.

Banks would face new obligations — verifying written designations before honoring remotely created checks, handling stop-payment rights, declining over-limit prepaid transactions without fees — and could lose processing revenue, though these are compliance costs rather than a change to their core business.
